Agricultural researchers are therefore turning to precision farming technologies — GPS-guided machinery, soil sensors, and data analytics — to maximize yields while minimizing resource waste.

Smart farming can drastically reduce the environmental footprint of agriculture. Sensors embedded in fields transmit real-time data on soil moisture, temperature, and nutrient levels, enabling farmers to (a) ________ fertilizer and water with surgical precision rather than blanket applications. Drones spray pesticides only where needed, cutting chemical use by up to 80 percent. Such efficiencies free up resources and reduce the runoff that pollutes rivers and coastal ecosystems.

Access to these technologies remains deeply unequal, however. Small-scale farmers in developing nations, who produce roughly 70 percent of the world's food, often lack the capital, connectivity, and training required.
